transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-03-14
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jared Kim (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Acme, Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Acme, CTO), Priya Singh (Acme, Platform Eng)

Summary: Quick sign-off on POC success criteria and acceptance tests; align on workload sizing for benchmarks, go/no-go thresholds, reporting format, and timeline for a dedicated benchmark run.

Topics: success criteria, latency/throughput targets, accuracy/regression thresholds, benchmark config, reporting template, timelines, security & data handling.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. This is the sign-off call on the POC success criteria, so we'll run through the thresholds, acceptance tests, and the plan for running the benchmarks. Jared's going to cover the benchmark config and reporting format.
[00:22] Lena: Thanks, Maya. Quick note — Tom and I just want to make sure the acceptance tests reflect our production mix, especially the long-form summarization flows.
[00:35] Jared: Yep, understood. We'll cover the 512-token and 2k-token profiles separately; those will map to your short chat and long summarize workloads.
[00:48] Tom: Also, security and data handling — SOC2, SSO, KMS — we did receive the security deck but want to double-check logs and retention during the POC.
[01:05] Maya: Good call. We'll include a clause: POC logs retained for 90 days in a Redwood-managed S3 with customer KMS keys; we'll share the security pack again after this call.
[01:20] Priya: Sounds good. On the workload profile, we will send 7 days of traces. Those include peak windows that are important for batching behavior.
[01:33] Jared: Perfect. So for the acceptance criteria we proposed — laying them out now:
[01:40] - Latency: 95th percentile tail latency under 250ms for the 512-token profile, and under 750ms for the 2k-token profile when running at sustained throughput equal to X% of your peak (we'll define X from your traces).
[02:01] - Throughput: ability to sustain 50 RPS for the short profile and 12 RPS for the long profile with <5% error rate.
[02:12] - Quality/accuracy: pass rate >= 97% on the curated eval set (we'll use your golden prompts + Redwood eval harness).
[02:25] - Resource/cost: per-token cost target not to exceed $0.0009/token (adjusted for quantization), with a 10% buffer for overhead.
[02:40] - Stability: no more than 1 incident (serve failures or OOM) in a 24-hour run; automatic fallback behavior exercised at least once.
[02:55] Maya: To be explicit: the go/no-go is if any of latency, throughput, or quality thresholds fail by more than 10% at the benchmark conditions, the pilot will be escalated rather than accepted. Small misses (<=10%) trigger mitigation work and follow-up benchmark.
[03:16] Lena: Can we capture the exact test harness — input distribution, concurrency pattern, and seed set for randomness — so we can reproduce results locally?
[03:27] Jared: Yes. We'll provide the benchmark template — it's the spreadsheet I shared (link: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/acme/poc-success-criteria-v3.xlsx). It includes the input distribution, concurrency patterns, warm-up period, and random seed details.
[03:45] Tom: On the latency numbers — the 95th pctl under 250ms for 512 tokens seems aggressive; what's the hardware assumption?
[03:55] Jared: That's on a dedicated A100-like pool, quantized int8 weights, and continuous KV cache warm. If you opt for hosted shared capacity, we expect p95 to be higher and cost per token lower, so we'll show both scenarios in the benchmark report.
[04:12] Priya: For the dedicated run, do you need us to provision any VPC peering or private endpoint? We want to simulate production networking.
[04:21] Maya: For the dedicated benchmark slot we'll set up a private endpoint; Redwood will request a short-lived peering token and we'll coordinate with Priya on IP ranges.
[04:34] Jared: Logging: we'll export per-token latencies, 50/90/95/99 percentiles, error types, and memory/GPU utilization every minute. The report will include cost breakdowns per model variant and quantization setting.
[04:52] Lena: Regarding quality — the 97% pass rate is on the golden prompts. How do we handle regressions where model scores drop but human reviewers say it's acceptable?
[05:05] Maya: We'll include a manual review gate: any failing cases in the eval will be triaged. If more than 10% of failures are deemed acceptable by your SME review, we mark quality as "conditional pass" and document the rationale.
[05:22] Tom: Ok. On timelines — what's realistic to get the benchmark run done? We need results before our internal decision meeting on 2025-03-28.
[05:33] Maya: If you can share traces by 2025-03-18, Redwood can run the benchmark week of 3/24 with results delivered by 3/26, leaving you time to review before 3/28.
[05:45] Priya: That works if we ship the traces by EOD 3/18. We'll aim for that.
[05:52] Jared: For the benchmark config specifics: warm-up 600 seconds, steady-state 3600 seconds for 24-hour window if you want stability, but for the acceptance test we'll run a 4-hour steady-state to control costs and still get representative p95. We'll also run an extended 24-hour run as a follow-up for durability metrics if needed.
[06:16] Maya: Great. Now walk us through the acceptance tests in the report format briefly — Jared?
[06:22] Jared: Sure. Report sections: Executive summary with pass/fail, Artifact links (benchmark config, raw logs, cost calc), Metrics table (latency percentiles, throughput, error rates, GPU util, per-token cost), Quality eval (pass rate + failing examples), Notes on environment (model version, quantization, kernel flags), and Recommendations. We'll flag any metric that misses thresholds by >10% as a hard-fail.
[06:46] Lena: For artifact sharing, we need a signed NDA addendum before Redwood can ingest traces into your environment; are we covered already?
[06:54] Maya: You're covered under the existing NDA but we'll attach a short POC addendum capturing retention and KMS details; I'll send that after the call.
[07:04] Tom: A couple technical questions: 1) KV cache warm — how do you measure warm vs cold? 2) How do you simulate prefix reuse?
[07:14] Jared: We instrument KV cache hit rate and will include a warm-up window where we replay prefixes to reach a steady-state hit rate. For the benchmark we'll report hit-rate curves and a baseline cold-run so you see extremes.
[07:28] Priya: When you compute per-token cost, does that include request orchestration and network egress?
[07:34] Jared: We'll include Redwood runtime overhead and GPU amortized costs. Network egress will be reported separately; if the test uses private peering egress is negligible.
[07:42] Maya: Also, one pragmatic note: if you want to test both 8-bit and 4-bit quant profiles we'll run them as separate model variants; 4-bit might reduce cost but could affect quality. We'll flag recommended profiles per workload.
[07:56] Lena: Let's be explicit in the document about the go/no-go definition so our procurement and legal teams can see it.
[08:03] Maya: Agreed. I'll draft a single-paragraph go/no-go: "POC PASS if at benchmark conditions the system meets or exceeds (latency p95, throughput, and quality) thresholds. Any metric missing more than 10% results in NO-GO and triggers remediation and a single retest window. Security non-compliance is immediate blocker."
[08:26] Tom: That reads fine. On reporting cadence, can we get a mid-run dashboard snapshot after the first hour?
[08:34] Jared: Yes — we'll publish an interim dashboard link and final artifacts.
[08:38] Lena: One more — our decision criteria also includes maintainability: how easy is it for our platform team to onboard models and update quantization profiles. Can we see a short runbook?
[08:49] Maya: We'll include a runbook snippet and an onboarding checklist in the deliverables.
[08:56] Priya: Network specifics: we'll provide CIDR blocks; do you need DNS entries?
[09:02] Jared: For private endpoint peering we just need the CIDR and a service account; Redwood will create the endpoint and coordinate keys.
[09:10] (brief cross talk)
[09:18] Jared: Ok, moving on to acceptance test scenarios — we'll enumerate:
[09:22] Scenario A: Short chat (512 tokens) steady-state at target throughput (50 RPS), p95 < 250ms, error rate <5%, quality pass >=97%.
[09:38] Scenario B: Long summarize (2k tokens) steady-state at 12 RPS, p95 < 750ms, same quality pass target.
[09:50] Scenario C: Spike test — 3x peak for 5 minutes to verify fallback and graceful degradation. No more than 10% increased error rate and latency should degrade predictably.
[10:04] Scenario D: Durability — 24-hour run that ensures no more than 1 incident and verifies memory stability.
[10:15] Maya: We'll mark Scenarios A+B as gate criteria for go/no-go. C and D are recommended for additional confidence; D will be run if you elect to proceed to longer pilot.
[10:27] Lena: About the benchmark harness — will logs include per-request model hash/version and quant flag so we can map regressions?
[10:36] Jared: Yes, each log line will include model version, quant flag, kernel flags, and a request id for traceability.
[10:44] Tom: On the cost calc, can you include a per-day extrapolation for 24/7 usage based on our traffic profile?
[10:51] Jared: We'll include daily and monthly extrapolations in the cost sheet.
[10:56] Priya: Any limitations on PII in the traces? We need to scrub patient identifiers.
[11:02] Maya: Please scrub or pseudonymize PII before upload; if you need Redwood to perform a scrub step, we can provide instructions but we won't accept raw PII without a data processing addendum.
[11:16] Lena: Got it.
[11:18] (pause)
[11:22] Maya: Alright let's confirm the final wording of success criteria live and I'll capture it — Jared, can you read the short list we'll put into the doc?
[11:30] Jared: Sure. Proposed success criteria phrasing: "Under the defined benchmark (short and long profiles), the system must meet: (1) p95 latency <250ms (short) / <750ms (long), (2) sustain throughput of 50 RPS (short) / 12 RPS (long) with <5% error rate, (3) quality pass rate >=97% on curated eval set, (4) per-token cost <= $0.0009/token (quantized baseline), (5) stability: <=1 incident in 24h. Any single criterion missed by >10% is a no-go."
[12:07] Lena: That looks good. We'll accept that wording subject to minor edits.
[12:12] Tom: For transparency, put the raw logs and cost calc in a read-only bucket with short-lived credentials.
[12:19] Maya: Yep — we'll create a signed URL bundle and a read-only S3 bucket scoped to the POC.
[12:26] Priya: Back to timelines: we'll aim to upload traces by 3/18; is 3/24 run slot realistic?
[12:33] Jared: Yes, assuming traces arrive by 3/18 we'll reserve a dedicated A100-equivalent slot on 3/24. We'll confirm exact time by 3/20.
[12:44] Maya: Anything else from the team?
[12:48] Lena: Just one tiny ask — in the final doc add a short table indicating what constitutes a "minor miss" vs "hard fail" so procurement can classify risks.
[12:59] Maya: Will do.
[13:02] Tom: Ok I'm good.
[13:06] Priya: Same.
[13:09] Maya: Great. Quick recap of next steps: 1) Redwood sends final success criteria doc + SOW + POC addendum (Maya) by 3/19. 2) Customer uploads traces by 3/18 (Priya). 3) Jared shares benchmark config + spreadsheet by 3/20. 4) Redwood runs dedicated benchmark week of 3/24 and delivers report by 3/26.
[13:34] (closing)
[13:36] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with artifact links.
[13:39] Lena: Thanks, talk soon.
[13:41] Tom: Thanks.
[13:43] Priya: Bye.

Notes/Artifacts referenced: benchmark spreadsheet (https://redwood.example/benchmarks/acme/poc-success-criteria-v3.xlsx), security pack link (https://redwood.example/security/acme-poc), sample SOW template (https://redwood.example/sow/poc-template.pdf)

End of transcript.
